title: PEER: Empowering Writing with Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper presents PEER (Paper Evaluation and Empowerment Resource), a web-based large language model tool designed to provide students with detailed, constructive, and motivating feedback on essays. The paper addresses a common educational problem: teachers often lack the time to give individualized, iterative writing feedback, which limits students’ opportunities to revise and improve. The authors position PEER as a way to support personalized writing instruction while also reducing teacher workload.

The intervention is an AI-assisted essay feedback system tailored to school writing tasks in German. Students upload or type essays, along with metadata such as essay type and grade level, and the system generates two feedback versions based on different prompts. Users indicate which feedback they prefer, and the system uses an Elo-rating approach to iteratively improve prompt selection. PEER is designed to support repeated revision cycles, allowing students to revise and request updated feedback multiple times. The technical approach relies on zero-shot prompting rather than a fine-tuned domain-specific model at this stage.

The context is real-world school use in Germany. Since launch in February 2023, more than 4000 essays had been uploaded, with strongest use among students in middle and upper school levels. The paper also reports qualitative feedback from teachers who experimented with the tool individually and in classrooms. However, it does not provide a controlled comparison against teacher feedback, peer feedback, automated writing evaluation, self-revision, or no-feedback conditions, nor does it report direct student learning outcome effects on writing quality.

The main conclusion is that PEER appears promising and addresses a perceived need for timely, individualized writing feedback in schools. Teachers reportedly valued its usability, respectful tone, and potential to support individualized learning and reduce workload, while also identifying weaknesses such as overly general suggestions, occasional grammar issues, and limitations in inclusive language handling. The authors emphasize that the project is still at an early stage and that future work will involve collecting teacher feedback data, fine-tuning the model, and conducting a more comprehensive school-based user study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a system/prototype paper with descriptive usage information and informal qualitative teacher feedback, but no clear empirical study design, no control or comparison group, no student outcome analysis, and no reported quantitative methodology for impact evaluation.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially beneficial but unquantified effects on writing support and teacher efficiency; because no effect sizes or controlled outcome evidence are reported, impact remains unclear rather than demonstrably positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Web-based LLM system (PEER) that analyzes student essays and generates detailed formative feedback with suggestions for revision; students can iteratively resubmit revised essays and compare alternative feedback prompts.
LLM-supported essay writing assistance in German, including OCR plus GPT post-processing and teacher-like writing feedback intended to support essay improvement across school essay types.
GenAI-supported personalized writing guidance framed as an AI tutor for repeated feedback cycles, though the implemented system is more feedback-oriented than full dialogue tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative teacher feedback suggesting that PEER provides timely, structured feedback that may reduce the tediousness of essay grading and support individualized instruction. However, no controlled comparison, workload time-study, or quantitative effect estimates are reported; evidence is based on anecdotal/early qualitative feedback from teachers after platform deployment with over 4,000 uploaded essays.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative feedback about usefulness, timeliness, and perceived workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that iterative LLM feedback could improve student essay writing and notes substantial real-world uptake (>4,000 essays uploaded, many in argumentation tasks), but it does not present pre/post writing scores, revision-quality metrics, or comparisons against teacher, peer, or no-feedback conditions. Qualitative teacher feedback was generally favorable regarding usefulness and tone, while also noting that feedback could be overly general and occasionally contain grammar or inclusivity-related errors.
finding.measure: Teacher qualitative assessments of feedback usefulness and observed limitations; platform usage counts
